title: Investment Winners: What the Data Says
subtitle: Five patterns from a first-buy-to-peak review of 146 completed holding episodes
body:
I wanted to answer a simple question with my own history: what did the investments that became meaningful winners actually do differently?

I reconstructed 146 usable holding episodes across 56 stocks and compared each first purchase with the highest split-adjusted daily price reached while the position was held. I then rolled repeated holdings of the same stock together so one idea appearing in several accounts would not dominate the result.

1. The clearest separator was time

Top-quartile stocks took a median 125 days to reach their peak, compared with 16.5 days for the rest. The strongest outcomes generally were not quick pops. They required enough time for operating momentum and market expectations to compound.

This does not mean every position should be held indefinitely. It means that selling solely because a stock has already risen can interrupt the part of the return distribution that matters most.

2. Repeatable winners clustered in scalable technology

Nine of the fourteen top-quartile stocks were associated with software, semiconductors, or compute infrastructure. APP, ALAB, IREN, NVDA, and RDDT were among the strongest names when ranked by the median result across eligible holding episodes.

The useful lesson is not to chase a sector label. These businesses shared the ability to translate demand into unusually rapid scaling. The operating mechanism mattered more than the category name.

3. Entry momentum helped, but did not explain success

The median sixty-trading-day momentum before purchase was positive for both groups: 40.8% for the eventual winners and 30.3% for the rest. Buying strength may have helped, but strength alone was a weak filter because many ordinary outcomes also began with strong price action.

Momentum appears more useful as confirmation of a business thesis than as a substitute for one.

4. Large givebacks were normal

The median top-quartile stock later retreated about 32% from its peak, almost the same as the rest of the sample. Several of the best long-term outcomes experienced substantially larger peak-to-later-price declines.

A large drawdown does not prove that the original thesis remains intact, but volatility by itself does not distinguish a broken company from a successful one. The business evidence still has to make that distinction.

5. Conviction appeared across repeated holdings

The winning group appeared in a median of three account episodes, compared with two for the rest. That suggests conviction tended to build around the better ideas. It does not prove that larger sizing caused the return; the causality may run the other way, with improving evidence leading to repeated purchases.

What I am changing

  • Give a strong thesis enough time to compound instead of optimizing for a quick payoff.
  • Treat price momentum as supporting evidence, not the investment case.
  • Expect volatility and review the operating thesis before reacting to a drawdown.
  • Track repeated conviction explicitly, while guarding against accidental concentration.
  • Keep studying both winners and failures so hindsight does not rewrite the original decision.

Limitations

This is a review of one portfolio history, not a controlled experiment. Some older positions lacked complete opening transactions and were excluded. The analysis measures price return from first buy to peak rather than total return or internal rate of return, and it remains exposed to survivorship, selection, and hindsight bias.

The point is not to produce a universal formula. It is to turn a personal record into a better decision process.

This is a personal retrospective, not financial advice.
